body:
The user's example contains the most useful lesson of all, once corrected. The "UBL issue" story frames a multibagger as one brilliant insight followed by an inevitable rise. The real Radico record shows something else: years of dead money, then a slow change in the business (premium mix, debt reduction, operating leverage) that anyone reading segment commentary and balance sheets in 2016–17 could see. It paid off through two engines at once, earnings and the multiple. NVIDIA shows the same pattern in a different form. In both cases the edge lay in **interpreting public data differently and having the temperament to hold through 50–75% drawdowns**, not in information others lacked. That shifts the investor's job. Finding the idea matters less than (a) a forensic filter that removes the Suzlons and Gensols, which tell the same story as the winners, (b) a valuation discipline that keeps both engines available, and (c) sizing and kill rules that let you survive the many bets that will fail, as base rates guarantee.

AI changes the cost of that work, not its nature. A retail investor with Claude, a Screener export, eight concall transcripts and a forensic prompt can now do in an evening the document-reading that once needed an analyst team. That makes the "reading between the lines" stage cheaper than it has ever been. The evidence also says that handing the *decision* to a model reproduces the classic retail failures of overtrading, concentration and invented numbers. The durable edge for an Indian investor seeking generational wealth is unglamorous: an index core, a concentrated but size-capped satellite of quality small and mid-cap compounders bought before their rerating, AI used as a tireless skeptic, and enough patience to let the rare 4% winner do what the other 96% cannot.

`case_study:wirecard-2020` | 2020-06-25 | tickers: DE-WDI | confidence: verified

Wirecard, a German payments processor in the DAX, peaked near EUR 190 in Sep 2018 (market cap ~EUR 24 bn). On 18 Jun 2020 auditor EY said EUR 1.9 bn of cash in Philippine trustee accounts could not be confirmed; on 22 Jun the company admitted it probably did not exist; CEO Markus Braun was arrested; insolvency on 25 Jun 2020; shares fell >98%. Visible flags years ahead: (1) FT Alphaville 'House of Wirecard' (2015) and Zatarra report (2016) questioned Asian acquisitions; (2) about half of profits came via 'third-party acquirers' (TPAs) in Asia that Wirecard did not control; (3) acquisitions at inflated prices (e.g., ~EUR 340 m for Indian assets in 2015, much of it to a Mauritius fund); (4) operating cash flow far weaker than EBITDA once customer-fund movements were stripped out; rising receivables; (5) FT's Dan McCrum's Jan 2019 whistleblower-based reports on Singapore round-tripping; (6) KPMG special audit (Apr 2020) could not verify revenues. Instead, BaFin banned short-selling (Feb-Apr 2019) and filed complaints against FT journalists. Lesson: regulator defence and DAX membership are not evidence; when profits sit in partners you can't audit and cash is held by 'trustees', require independent confirmation. Short sellers and journalists were right for 5 years.

**Lesson:** Third-party-held cash + unauditable partners = disqualifier
**Spotted early by:** Dan McCrum (FT), Zatarra, short sellers (e.g., Fraser Perring)
**Links:** illustrates -> `insight:short-seller-reports-outcomes`, illustrates -> `insight:auditor-exit-signal`, illustrates -> `insight:disqualifiers`

`case_study:page-industries-2007-2022` · tickers: PAGEIND · confidence: verified

No splits. First listed week Mar 2007 ₹272 → ATH ₹53,453 (Oct 2022) ≈197x; ₹31,065 on 19 Nov 2026 (−42% from ATH). Twin engine: P/E 26.6 → 81.4 (3.1x) × implied EPS ~64x (TTM EPS ₹14.9 → ₹657); the business did most of the work. Drawdowns: −41% (2008), −38% (2015–16), −52% (Aug 2018–Apr 2020). Early signal: exclusive Jockey licensee for India since 1994 (renewed to 2030); revenue CAGR ~35% FY04–15 with a new product line almost every year; ROCE 50–70% with negligible debt; P/E fell to ~13 at end-2008, so a fast grower was briefly priced like a commodity company. Investors who caught it (2008–2010) mostly just held. Ended/stalled: after the 2022 peak, FY23 trade destocking and weak demand cut TTM EPS from ₹658 to ₹458; EPS recovered to ₹708 by 2026 (above 2022), but P/E fell from ~81 to ~44, so 4 years of EPS growth were erased by de-rating. Sales CAGR slowed to ~11% (FY15–26). Lesson: brand-licence compounders bought at 13–30x make money; at 80x+ the next four years depend entirely on growth not slowing. Licence concentration (Jockey International) is a permanent tail risk.

Key data: **start_year**: 2007; **end_year**: 2022; **start_price**: 272; **end_price**: 53453; **price_nov2026**: 31065; **multiple**: ~197x; **pe_start**: 26.6; **pe_end**: 81.4; **eps_multiple_implied**: ~64x; **max_drawdown**: -52% (2018-20); **early_signals**: exclusive licence, 60%+ ROCE, P/E ~13 in 2008, new categories yearly; **ended**: growth slowdown FY23 + P/E 81→44; **lesson**: de-rating can erase years of EPS growth

body:
1. **Our edge is the inattention premium, not public factors** (#16, #3, #13-15). Published anomalies lose about 58% after publication, and the survivors are crowded. What persists is information that is public but costly to process: filing diffs, concall Q&A, supplier links, late or crowded announcements. Indian small and mid caps are the least-read part of the market, and that is where our reading effort pays.
2. **Process beats intuition** (#35, #36, #32, #33). Mechanical scorecards match or beat experts. Dated probability forecasts with Brier scores make luck and skill visible, and our own ranges are probably too narrow.
3. **Capital-allocation events carry base rates** (#7, #18, #20, #21, #22). Equity issuance, asset sprees and big acquisitions are negative on average. Value-stock buybacks and first dividends are positive. Use these as priors in every thesis.
4. **India governance has academic backing** (#25, #26, #27). Pledging predicts crashes, low-ownership group affiliates leak value, and group IPOs are overpriced on listing day.
5. **Backtest hygiene** (#4, #1). Every rule we test on Indian data needs t>3 or a hold-out sample, and every variant tried has to be counted.

body:
- `g_t` fades linearly from `growth` (year 1) to `growth_end` (year N). The NOPAT margin moves linearly from today's to `margin_end`.
- `FCF = NOPAT × (1 − g / ROIIC)`: growth has to be paid for (value-driver formula; `insight:flag-high-pe-context`).
- `TV = NOPAT_N × (1+tg) × (1 − tg/ROIC_T) / (r − tg)`. Equity = PV + recurring non-operating income perpetuity + non-operating assets − net debt.
- `EPS_t` scales with operating NOPAT + recurring other income. Treasury income on net cash is held flat.
- 5-year multiple = (EPS₅ × exit P/E + distributed FCF per share) ÷ price. Set `"exit_pe": "dcf"` to use the DCF-consistent multiple instead.
- 5-year probabilities: each scenario gets a lognormal spread (σ = `dispersion`, default 0.30) and the blow-up is a point mass.
